Incorrect. The generic collision estimate is about 2^(n/2), rather than half of the full 2^n search space.

questions.prompt: Which combination is necessary for the classical one-time-pad confidentiality claim? Select all that apply.
options: Publishing the pad after each ciphertext is transmitted
No reuse of pad material across messages
Truly random secret pad at least as long as the message
Keeping the pad secret from the adversary
explanations: Publication reveals the plaintext to anyone retaining the ciphertext.
Reuse violates the one-time assumption.
The pad must supply sufficient independent random secret material.
Secrecy of the pad is essential.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism fits a public-verification requirement for an artifact publisher’s approval?
options: A checksum hosted beside the artifact with no authenticated origin
A governed digital signature with trusted public-key binding
A shared MAC key distributed to every public verifier
Encryption with one shared key given to all downloaders
explanations: A mutable unauthenticated checksum lacks publisher binding.
Verifiers can check without receiving signing capability.
Public holders of a MAC key can generate tags themselves.
Shared encryption does not distinguish a specific publisher’s approval.

questions.prompt: Which failure can remain even when an envelope-encrypted archive uses strong algorithms?
options: The encrypted data keys are stored beside their ciphertext objects
Different objects use different data-encryption keys
An application identity is authorised to unwrap every data key without a justified need
The wrapping service maintains a key version identifier
explanations: Wrapped keys can be stored with ciphertext under an appropriate design.
Per-object keys can support separation and lifecycle control.
Key-service authorisation can defeat the intended confidentiality boundary.
Version identity is useful for selecting and managing keys.

questions.prompt: What is the correct role pairing for the final NIST post-quantum families named here?
options: ML-KEM is a digital-signature scheme; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA establish shared secrets
ML-KEM establishes key material; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA provide signatures
ML-KEM signs artifacts; ML-DSA encrypts bulk database files
ML-KEM establishes key material; ML-DSA encrypts payloads; SLH-DSA signs artifacts
explanations: Incorrect. This reverses the KEM and signature roles.
The standards specify a KEM and two signature families respectively.
This swaps roles and invents bulk-encryption behaviour.
Incorrect. ML-DSA is a signature family, not a bulk-payload encryption scheme.

questions.prompt: A cloned device image repeats the internal state of its deterministic simulation PRNG, which is used for private keys. What is the principal issue?
options: A longer ciphertext tag will independently make those keys unpredictable
Reissuing certificates with new serial numbers repairs the repeated private-key values
Predictable or repeated key material because the generator and state lifecycle are unsuitable
Changing file permissions after generation repairs the repeated key values
explanations: Tag length cannot create missing key entropy.
Incorrect. Certificate metadata does not add entropy to repeated generated keys.
Cryptographic key generation needs appropriate entropy, generator construction and state management.
Permissions can limit access but do not repair already repeated secrets.

questions.prompt: A receiver decrypts an AEAD record and applies its command before checking the tag. Which correction is required?
options: Check the tag only if the command later fails
Use a public nonce as proof that authentication will succeed
Store the invalid plaintext as trusted evidence because decryption succeeded
Make successful authentication a prerequisite for releasing or acting on the protected plaintext
explanations: A failed or successful business action does not validate the tag.
Nonce visibility says nothing about tag validity.
Decryption output alone is not trusted plaintext.
Unauthenticated data must not drive the protected operation.

questions.prompt: Which migration priority follows from long-lived sensitive traffic that could be recorded today?
options: Wait until a practical attack is observed against this organisation’s exact traffic
Assess required secrecy lifetime and the dependencies that must transition before future cryptanalytic exposure
Assume all symmetric and asymmetric mechanisms fail identically under every quantum attack
Prioritize only short-lived public data while deferring long-lived recorded secrets
explanations: Observed exploitation can be too late for previously captured data.
Retention risk and migration lead time can make action necessary before a practical attack arrives.
Quantum effects differ by problem and construction.
Incorrect. Recorded sensitive traffic with a long confidentiality lifetime can create an earlier migration need.

questions.prompt: Which description correctly distinguishes a digital signature from a generic encryption operation?
options: A signature scheme has its own generation/verification construction and needs a trusted signing-key binding
A valid signature always proves the human signer personally read the complete document
Every signature is produced by running any encryption algorithm backwards
Signature verification alone confirms that the message is still timely and authorised
explanations: Scheme correctness, identity binding and use context all matter.
Human intent and key custody require additional evidence.
This is not a valid general model for modern signature schemes.
Freshness and business authority require contextual checks.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes elliptic-curve mechanisms?
options: Both provide identical protocol roles because their names start with EC
ECDH is password hashing; ECDSA is bulk symmetric encryption
ECDH supports key agreement; ECDSA supports digital signatures
A 256-bit curve parameter automatically equals the security strength of any 256-bit public-key modulus
explanations: A shared mathematical family does not make their interfaces interchangeable.
Those are not their defined roles.
These are distinct constructions using elliptic-curve mathematics for different purposes.
Cross-family bit lengths are not interchangeable security-strength measures.

questions.prompt: A proposal uses QKD and claims no endpoint authentication is needed. What is the flaw?
options: Key distribution does not remove authenticated-endpoint/classical-channel and implementation requirements
QKD makes compromised endpoint software trustworthy
A physical channel guarantees that applications always use keys correctly
QKD is simply another name for every post-quantum signature algorithm
explanations: The overall system still needs authenticated peers and secure operation under the QKD design.
An endpoint compromise is not repaired by key-distribution technology.
Key use and application authority remain separate responsibilities.
QKD and conventional post-quantum algorithms are different approaches.

questions.prompt: A chain validates to a trusted root but its certificate names a different service. What should the relying client do?
options: Accept because root trust overrides the expected service identity
Accept if the public key length is sufficient
Reject the peer identity mismatch under the application validation rules
Treat the mismatch only as a certificate-expiration issue
explanations: Path trust and identity matching are separate required checks.
Strong key size does not bind the wrong name to the expected service.
Trust in the issuer does not make every issued identity the intended peer.
A name mismatch is independent of the validity interval.

questions.prompt: Why does a self-signed root certificate not independently prove that its operator is trustworthy?
options: Every root must obtain an online status response for each leaf
A self-signature independently establishes that the root's identity vetting is reliable
Its trust-anchor status comes from the relying party’s authorised trust decision
A self-signature cannot be mathematically verified
explanations: Status design is separate and varies by trust architecture.
Incorrect. Self-verification does not supply external evidence about the operator or its practices.
A self-signature cannot establish an external trust relationship by itself.
Its signature may be mathematically valid; that is not external identity proof.

questions.prompt: A client certificate authenticates an engineering workstation through mutual TLS. Which decision still belongs to the application?
options: Whether the TLS record has any integrity mechanism
Whether the peer certificate parses under the TLS library's certificate-encoding rules
Whether the client possesses any private-key capability used by the handshake
Whether that identity may perform the requested operational action
explanations: TLS already provides record protection in its defined protocol.
Incorrect. Certificate parsing is part of the protocol validation machinery, not the application's decision about permitted operations.
Successful certificate authentication provides evidence of the relevant key capability under the protocol.
Authentication establishes an identity claim; authorisation scopes permitted actions.

questions.prompt: A validly signed status response is outside the accepted freshness interval. Which conclusion follows?
options: The server private key is necessarily compromised
Its signature alone does not establish current revocation status
The certificate must be treated as never having existed
A valid signature makes status timeless
explanations: Staleness alone does not prove key compromise.
Status authenticity and currentness are separate conditions.
Stale status does not erase certificate existence.
A signature protects the statement, including its time context.

questions.prompt: A status service outage blocks a critical gateway. What should govern fail-open versus fail-closed behaviour?
options: A universal rule that every operational service must always fail open
A preapproved risk and continuity policy with tested consequences
A universal rule that certificate expiry and status outage are identical events
Whichever operator first notices the outage without escalation criteria
explanations: Always opening can admit revoked identities and ignores service risk.
The decision balances defined trust and availability requirements under authorised design.
Expiry and inability to obtain current status are distinct conditions.
Ad hoc decisions undermine the authority and failure model.

questions.prompt: An HSM key is non-exportable but an attacker controls a caller allowed to sign arbitrary releases. What remains exposed?
options: Only extraction of the raw private-key bytes could permit release-signing misuse
The signing operation can be misused without exporting the private key
No attack is possible because key bytes cannot leave
The caller's privilege becomes harmless because the HSM checks key storage internally
explanations: Incorrect. A permitted caller can misuse signing operations without exporting the key.
Operation authority is itself a consequential capability.
Non-exportability is not a complete use-authorisation control.
Incorrect. Protected storage does not replace application-level control over authorized signing requests.

questions.prompt: Which design most directly implements dual control for key destruction?
options: Two copies of the same secret are stored on one account
One custodian enters two passwords they personally know
Two separately authorised custodians must approve and execute the controlled ceremony
The same custodian confirms the request twice in separate sessions
explanations: Copies under one authority do not establish participation separation.
One person retaining both factors does not create two-person control.
Multiple independent authorised participants constrain the action.
Incorrect. Two confirmations by one actor do not implement independent participation.

questions.prompt: A new wrapping-key version is activated. What must be checked before destroying the old one?
options: Only that new encryption requests can use the new wrapping version
Whether retained data keys still depend on the old version and have a verified recovery/migration path
Only that new writes select the new version
Only that the old version is no longer the default for new writes
explanations: Incorrect. Historical objects may still require the old wrapping key even when new requests succeed.
Historical dependencies can remain even when new operations use a new key.
New-write behaviour does not prove old-object recoverability.
Incorrect. Removing default status does not demonstrate that every dependent historical object has a valid recovery path.

questions.prompt: A private signing key is escrowed with a recovery provider. Which claim needs particular qualification?
options: Availability of a documented recovery path
The mathematical ability to verify a correctly generated signature
Exclusive attribution of all signatures to the original signer
Existence of a public verification key
explanations: Escrow may provide recovery, though its effectiveness needs evidence.
The signature can still verify mathematically.
Another party with signing capability affects custody and attribution claims.
Escrow does not remove the public key.

questions.prompt: Which evidence is needed beyond a scheduled key-rotation success message? Select all that apply.
options: The treatment of old key copies and relevant backups
An assumption that every historical object was re-encrypted automatically
Confirmation that unauthorised identities cannot invoke the new key
Recovery of representative retained ciphertext under the intended key versions
explanations: Old copies and dependencies determine residual exposure.
Migration behaviour must be established rather than assumed.
New key authority must match the security design.
Rotation must preserve authorised historical access where required.

questions.prompt: A certificate is within its dates but its private key was compromised and revoked. Which property is insufficient for acceptance?
options: The relying party’s current approved revocation policy
The permitted certificate-purpose check
The certificate’s unexpired validity interval
The expected peer identity comparison
explanations: The revocation policy is relevant to the decision, not a substitute for dates.
Purpose validation is also necessary and distinct.
Being unexpired does not override revocation.
Identity matching remains necessary but cannot alone override revocation.

questions.prompt: What is the security significance of adding a new broadly trusted CA root to every workstation?
options: It grants no new trust unless each leaf is also manually installed
It automatically rotates every existing private key
It expands the set of issuer statements those relying parties may accept
It affects only TLS performance and creates no additional identity-assertion authority
explanations: Path validation can accept leaves through the new root without manual leaf installation.
Installing a root does not rotate other keys.
Trust-store changes alter an authority boundary.
Incorrect. Broad root trust can authorize chains and identities, not merely change performance.

questions.prompt: An archive’s decryption permission is revoked, but all keys and backups remain. Can this alone demonstrate cryptographic erasure?
options: No; access revocation is not evidence that the necessary key material was destroyed
Yes; backup keys are irrelevant to recoverability
Yes; every authorisation change deletes ciphertext mathematically
Only if the current user interface hides the archived records
explanations: Recovery-capable key copies and plaintext must be considered.
Backup keys can preserve decryptability.
Permissions and key destruction are different events.
Interface visibility is not sanitisation evidence.

questions.prompt: A signed document is checked years after its signing certificate expired. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Declare every signature invalid retroactively on certificate expiry
Re-sign the original as the former signer without authorisation
Ignore all certificate and timestamp evidence because the signature bytes match
Evaluate historical validation evidence, time and trust context rather than treating expiry alone as proof the earlier signature was invalid
explanations: Later expiry does not itself establish invalidity at signing time.
Creating a new unauthorised signature is not validation.
Mathematical verification alone does not resolve historical trust.
Historical validity needs preserved evidence and policy.

questions.prompt: A registration authority’s principal role in a conventional PKI division is to do what?
options: Guarantee that a private key can never be misused
Act as the relying application’s complete authorisation engine
Validate applicant identity/request conditions under the issuance process
Encrypt every TLS application record
explanations: No role label guarantees absence of key misuse.
Application authorisation remains a separate function.
Registration supports the issuer’s decision through defined verification.
TLS record protection is performed by communicating endpoints.

questions.prompt: A gateway reports every new certificate as not yet valid after a restart. Other peers validate those certificates. Which evidence should be checked first?
options: Whether the service certificate has a different extended key usage despite other peers succeeding
Whether the issuing CA has published a newer CRL despite the explicit date error
Whether the server offers the expected TLS cipher suite despite the reported validity failure
The gateway’s trusted time and the certificate validity timestamps
explanations: Purpose constraints matter, but do not explain a uniform not-yet-valid result across otherwise valid new certificates.
Revocation matters, but the stated not-yet-valid diagnosis first points to validity timestamps and local time.
Cipher negotiation is distinct from certificate time validity; investigate the reported condition first.
A clock reset can systematically affect validity checks; compare actual times before changing trust.

questions.prompt: An analyst may submit selected plaintexts to an encryption interface and inspect the outputs. Which adversary capability is described?
options: Chosen-plaintext access
Ciphertext-only access
Private-key recovery
Second-preimage access
explanations: The analyst chooses original inputs and observes their encryptions.
Ciphertext-only access does not include selecting plaintext queries.
Access to the oracle does not itself establish key recovery.
Second-preimage is a hash attack goal, not this access model.

questions.prompt: Under the stated repeated-keystream XOR model, what is C1 XOR C2?
options: The secret key independently of both plaintexts
explanations: The second bit differs and must be 1; the third is equal and must be 0.
1010 XOR 0110 equals 1100, which equals P1 XOR P2 under reuse.
The common keystream cancels; the result is a plaintext relationship.
The first bits differ, so the first output bit cannot be 0.
questions.exhibit:
Synthetic training exhibit; no live system or actual organisation was tested.

C1=1010
C2=0110
Both use the same four keystream bits.

questions.prompt: An attacker has stolen password verifiers and can compute guesses locally. Which existing control may no longer limit their guess rate?
options: The login server’s online per-account throttle
A costly password derivation configured in the captured verifier scheme
A separately protected secret required to verify each guess
High entropy in the actual chosen password
explanations: Offline computation bypasses the online request interface.
A per-guess derivation cost still affects offline computation.
An unavailable required secret can constrain offline verification under the design.
An unpredictable password still expands the search difficulty.

questions.prompt: An application uses hash(secret || message) as an invented MAC. What is the strongest engineering response?
options: Replace the ad hoc construction with a vetted standard MAC/protocol and validate encoding and key use
Simply reverse the concatenation and assume a security proof follows
Increase the message length until extension attacks are impossible
Hide the hash algorithm name from users
explanations: A standard construction addresses a defined security model; integration still matters.
Another ad hoc construction is not justified by reversing inputs.
Longer messages do not establish MAC security.
Algorithm secrecy is not the required protection.

questions.prompt: Different malformed encrypted requests reveal distinct padding outcomes. What combination makes this a concern?
options: The existence of any public certificate regardless of the decryption interface
A queryable decryption-related oracle combined with vulnerable construction/processing behaviour
Different ciphertext lengths alone with no distinguishable secret-dependent response
Only a password-salt difference unrelated to the decryption endpoint
explanations: Public certificates do not explain padding-dependent response leakage.
Adaptive feedback can reveal information under a vulnerable design.
Incorrect. The concern needs an oracle-like observable behavior that reveals relevant processing outcomes.
Incorrect. A separate verifier setting does not establish the supplied padding-oracle mechanism.

questions.prompt: Error messages are identical, but timing still depends on secret-sensitive processing. Which assertion is justified?
options: The primitive’s public specification must be secret to repair the issue
A fixed random delay mathematically eliminates every timing leak
One observable distinction remains and needs threat-model-specific assessment
The implementation is proven constant time because the strings match
explanations: Implementation leakage is not repaired by hiding the algorithm.
Noise can complicate measurements without eliminating the signal.
Different channels must be assessed; exploitability needs further evidence.
Text equality does not imply equal timing or memory behaviour.

questions.prompt: A previously valid signed command is accepted a second time. Which missing property is most directly implicated?
options: The signature’s mathematical ability to verify
Replay/freshness enforcement for that transaction
Collision resistance of an unrelated file checksum
Confidentiality of the public verification key
explanations: The signature may be perfectly valid while the replay is unacceptable.
The same authentic statement can be reused unless the protocol constrains it.
A separate checksum does not govern transaction repetition.
Verification keys are normally public.

questions.prompt: A client retries a failed secure handshake by disabling certificate validation. Which attack opportunity does this create?
options: The server’s private key is automatically rotated
The client necessarily gains stronger forward secrecy
The fallback ensures the same peer identity was authenticated
An induced failure can trigger a weaker unauthenticated fallback
explanations: The client setting does not rotate the server key.
Disabling validation does not strengthen peer authentication or forward secrecy.
The fallback removes the stated identity check.
An adversary can target fallback behaviour to bypass the intended trust check.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes a collision search from a second-preimage search?
options: Both always require the attacker to recover a secret encryption key
Second-preimage search may freely choose both documents before their digests are fixed
Collision search necessarily reveals the plaintext of an encrypted message
Collision search may choose both distinct inputs; second-preimage search must match the digest of a specified input
explanations: Hash attack goals do not inherently involve an encryption key.
That describes the freer collision setting.
A hash collision is not decryption.
The target constraints define different attack goals.

questions.prompt: A relay forwards a legitimate authentication exchange to another endpoint without learning the password. Which design property directly addresses the misplaced exchange context?
options: Only increasing password complexity without binding the exchange to its intended endpoint and role
Appropriate endpoint/channel binding and phishing-resistant protocol design
Only encrypting the password database backup
Only increasing the password’s maximum allowed length
explanations: Incorrect. A relay can forward a valid exchange without learning or guessing the password.
Binding authentication to the intended endpoint/channel can constrain relays.
Backup encryption addresses another exposure path.
A relay can forward proof without guessing a long password.

questions.prompt: A stolen ticket permits access until expiry even after a password change. What should the response investigate?
options: Only whether the ticket was issued before the password change
The ticket/session invalidation model, scope and remaining authority
Only whether the new password contains more characters
Only whether the ticket is encrypted while stored on the original endpoint
explanations: Incorrect. Issue time is relevant context, but effective invalidation and remaining session authority must be examined.
Password changes do not necessarily revoke all already-issued artifacts.
Password strength does not alone revoke an existing valid ticket.
Incorrect. Storage encryption does not revoke a stolen usable ticket already held by an attacker.

questions.prompt: A content checksum differs from its trusted expected value. Which conclusion is supported immediately?
options: The hashing algorithm has definitely been broken
The original file’s confidentiality was necessarily lost
A named attacker necessarily modified the file
The compared content does not match the trusted reference under that check
explanations: Corruption or different input is a simpler possible cause.
Integrity disagreement does not by itself establish disclosure.
Attribution requires more than a checksum difference.
Mismatch establishes disagreement; causation needs further evidence.

questions.prompt: Which factors belong in assessment of a cryptographic side channel? Select all that apply.
options: The claim that mathematical correctness alone proves no leakage
Whether secret-dependent processing affects those observations
The implementation and platform assumptions of the mitigation
The adversary’s access to timing/cache/power or other observations
explanations: Correct outputs do not prove absence of side-channel information.
Leakage needs a relationship to protected information.
Mitigation effectiveness depends on the actual environment.
Available observations determine the attack model.

questions.prompt: A bearer API token is logged in plaintext on an endpoint. Which protection does TLS on the network fail to provide here?
options: Peer authentication under the correctly validated TLS mode
Protection of the token after endpoint logging exposes it
Confidentiality against a passive observer of that correctly protected link
Integrity of the protected transport records within the TLS connection
explanations: Correctly configured TLS can authenticate its peers under the mode.
TLS does not encrypt or authorise later endpoint log access.
The stated link protection can remain sound despite endpoint leakage.
TLS can protect record integrity within its scope.

questions.prompt: A ransomware decryption tool restores some files. What is still needed before declaring trustworthy recovery?
options: Assume restored bytes prove the attacker has no remaining access
Immediately delete all logs because recovery makes investigation unnecessary
Validate restored data and services, remove intrusion paths and re-establish trusted identities and evidence
Treat successful decryption as a complete backup strategy
explanations: Access may persist through credentials, services or other paths.
Evidence can be essential to understand scope and prevent recurrence.
File access is one part of recovery; system trust and operational validation remain.
A one-off tool is not a resilient backup/recovery programme.

questions.prompt: The same authentication key and response format are accepted in opposite protocol roles. Which design issue should be assessed?
options: Only whether the same response is transmitted over an encrypted channel
A requirement to make all public verification keys secret
Reflection or cross-role misuse due to missing context and key separation
Only whether the response encoding is canonical
explanations: Incorrect. Channel encryption does not by itself bind a response to the correct opposite protocol role.
Public-key secrecy is not the appropriate protection.
Roles and direction need unambiguous binding under the protocol.
Incorrect. Canonical encoding does not supply the missing role/context separation.

questions.prompt: A classical substitution cipher retains language letter frequencies. Which analysis exploits that surviving structure?
options: Frequency analysis
A guarantee of successful preimage recovery against every modern hash
A proof that all authenticated encryption leaks the same statistics
Public-key certificate path validation
explanations: The observed symbol distribution can expose structure in a weak substitution scheme.
Hash preimage resistance is a different problem.
The weakness is tied to the construction and its surviving structure, not every modern scheme.
Certificate validation does not analyse language frequencies.

questions.prompt: Two rack supplies use two outlets behind one upstream breaker. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The rack has fully independent end-to-end power paths
The upstream breaker remains a common power dependency
The outlet labels prove separate utility sources
The second supply eliminates every maintenance outage risk
explanations: Independence must be traced beyond the outlet and supply.
Both paths can be lost through the same upstream element.
Labels do not establish the physical topology.
Maintenance of the shared element can affect both paths.

questions.prompt: One valid badge event corresponds to two people entering together. Which boundary failed most directly?
options: The camera necessarily failed because it recorded the second entrant
The access database necessarily lost its record
The badge’s encryption algorithm necessarily failed
Binding each physical entry to an authorised person
explanations: The camera supplied evidence rather than failed in the stated observation.
The record exists; the issue is the extra physical entrant.
The authorised badge may have worked exactly as designed.
Tailgating can bypass the intended one-person entry decision.

questions.prompt: A proposed lock configuration would prevent required emergency egress on power loss. What is the appropriate design response?
options: Accept the obstruction because fail-secure always overrides egress
Retain the obstructing lock behavior because the access-control specification passed its normal-entry test
Coordinate a compliant security and life-safety solution with the responsible qualified authority
Disable every access-control function permanently without review
explanations: A security label does not override life-safety obligations.
Incorrect. Normal entry does not validate emergency egress and power-loss behavior.
Physical protection must be designed with applicable safe-egress requirements.
An unreviewed blanket removal does not solve the actual design requirement.

questions.prompt: A camera covers a doorway but recorded footage cannot distinguish entrants under normal night lighting. What evidence is missing?
options: Only proof that the camera delivers a continuous video stream
Only the design drawing's nominal field-of-view coverage
Demonstrated image usefulness under the actual operating conditions
Only that recorded files meet the configured retention duration
explanations: Incorrect. A stream can be available while image quality fails the required identification purpose.
Incorrect. Coverage on paper does not demonstrate usable recorded detail under actual night conditions.
Coverage must be assessed for the intended identification/observation task.
Incorrect. Retention preserves recordings but does not establish that the retained images distinguish entrants.

questions.prompt: Two telecom providers enter through the same vulnerable duct. Which concern should the assessment record?
options: Different contracts guarantee independent hazard exposure
A second invoice proves a separate building entrance
A shared physical path can defeat apparent provider diversity
Encryption removes the availability impact of duct damage
explanations: Provider names do not establish route independence.
Billing evidence does not show the physical route.
Contract diversity and physical diversity are different properties.
Encryption cannot carry traffic through a severed shared path.

questions.prompt: A UPS supports a load for the design bridging interval. Which additional evidence is needed for a longer outage claim?
options: Only a successful test lasting the already-proven bridging interval
A claim that all UPS systems provide unlimited runtime
The complete generation, transfer, fuel and downstream support/recovery design
Only the UPS's maximum output power rating
explanations: Incorrect. Repeating a shorter test does not establish energy supply and recovery for the longer outage.
Stored energy is finite and depends on the load and condition.
Longer continuity depends on the complete engineered support path.
Incorrect. Power capacity does not establish the energy and upstream arrangements required for sustained operation.

questions.prompt: Room-average temperature is normal but a rack inlet is above its approved range. What should guide diagnosis?
options: A rule that all sensors must report identical values
Local inlet, load, airflow and sensor evidence
Increasing room cooling output without checking the affected rack's airflow path
The assumption that room average invalidates every local alarm
explanations: Different locations can legitimately have different values.
The local equipment condition and measurement context need investigation.
Incorrect. A local inlet problem can arise from recirculation or obstruction even when overall room cooling appears adequate.
Averages can hide local extremes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a remote OFF indication is correct?
options: It permits any user to begin electrical work
It proves every energy source has been removed
It does not alone establish the physical isolation and stored-energy conditions required for safe work
It is always equivalent to the applicable hazardous-energy verification procedure
explanations: Competence and work authority are not conferred by a display.
Other sources and stored energy may remain.
Control indication and verified safe isolation are different evidence.
Applicable procedures require their own authorised verification.

questions.prompt: An intrusion sensor frequently alarms on legitimate activity and staff begin ignoring it. Which improvement addresses the control as a system?
options: Suppress all alarms permanently to reduce workload
Raise the alarm threshold until routine events disappear without checking missed detections
Review sensing conditions, tuning, triage and response performance together
Count the installed sensor as effective regardless of response
explanations: Blanket suppression removes detection rather than improving it.
Incorrect. Tuning must evaluate detection and response outcomes, not merely reduce the displayed count.
Detection and acted-upon response need to work under real conditions.
Installation alone is not effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Which factors belong in a facility common-cause assessment? Select all that apply.
options: The assumption that different equipment serial numbers prove independence
Shared upstream utility and control dependencies
Maintenance states that temporarily remove separation
Physical co-location of nominally redundant routes
explanations: Identity of equipment does not prove independent failure paths.
Upstream support can defeat multiple downstream components.
The operational state can change the failure model.
A local event can affect co-located routes.

questions.prompt: A contractor has building-entry permission for a delivery. Which additional permission should not be assumed?
options: A time-limited access condition if explicitly assigned
Permission to present the issued entry credential under its stated scope
The existence of a sponsoring delivery workflow if documented
Authority to access every controlled rack and perform maintenance
explanations: An explicitly assigned time limit is a stated condition, not an inferred expansion.
This is the narrow permission stated in the scenario.
A documented sponsor can be part of the authorised workflow.
Physical entry scope does not automatically grant equipment or work authority.

questions.prompt: A failed server is sent for repair with an asset tag on its chassis. What additional information matters for data custody?
options: A presumption that failed equipment cannot retain information
Only the server-level asset record without identifying contained media
Only a statement that the operating system no longer boots
The data-bearing components actually present and their sanitisation/protection status
explanations: Failure of a server does not imply erasure of its media.
Incorrect. Media identity and data disposition can require more detail than the chassis inventory.
Incorrect. Boot failure does not establish that stored information is inaccessible or appropriately controlled.
Storage and embedded components may retain sensitive information independently of the chassis tag.

questions.prompt: A leak detector produces a local indicator but no responsible team receives or acts on it. What is the main control gap?
options: Detection is not connected to an effective assessment and response workflow
Every leak detector automatically isolates all sources
The sensor’s existence proves the water risk is controlled
An unacknowledged indicator establishes successful recovery
explanations: A sensor alone cannot deliver the intended response outcome.
Isolation behaviour is design-specific and cannot be assumed.
Presence is not evidence of action or risk treatment effectiveness.
Recovery needs actual condition and service evidence.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claimed emergency communications capability?
options: An assumption that normal email always remains available
A contact list that has never been checked
An approved exercise showing roles, alternate communications and accountability under the stated outage conditions
Only confirmation that a secondary communication channel was purchased
explanations: The event may affect the normal communication dependency.
Unverified contacts may fail when needed.
A representative exercised workflow supplies stronger operational evidence.
Incorrect. Provisioning alone does not prove the channel works under the relevant failure and staffing conditions.

questions.prompt: A cybersecurity change alters HVAC and fire-system interactions. Who should evaluate acceptance?
options: Only the procurement team that bought the controller
Only the software developer because the change is expressed in code
The responsible qualified system/life-safety authorities within the approved change process
Any operator who can silence the resulting alarm
explanations: Procurement ownership alone is not technical acceptance competence.
Software form does not remove physical consequence or discipline requirements.
Cross-system safety and operational effects require the appropriate authority and expertise.
Access to an alarm control is not design authority.

questions.prompt: A physical-security report states only “the building is insecure.” What would make the finding actionable?
options: A statement that all facilities share exactly the same requirements
An observed boundary failure, consequence, responsible owner and closure evidence
A higher severity rating with no affected asset, condition or consequence
A larger set of site observations without linking them to a requirement or corrective owner
explanations: Site, service and jurisdiction requirements differ.
Specific evidence and accountable treatment enable a defensible response.
Incorrect. Severity needs an evidence-linked finding to guide corrective action.
Incorrect. Evidence must support the specific condition, impact and action rather than merely accumulate.

questions.prompt: A system meets a documented 60 second alarm requirement but operators need 10 seconds for the intended response. Which conclusion is most precise?
options: The implementation must be nonconforming to the stated 60 second requirement
Validation necessarily passes because one test passed
Verification may pass while validation of the stakeholder need fails
The test proves that the stakeholder need was correctly elicited
explanations: The implementation may conform exactly to the wrong requirement.
A passing specification test does not establish the need was correct.
Conformance to the written requirement is distinct from fitness for intended use.
The requirement itself can be inadequate.

questions.prompt: An unauthorised edit fails through the UI but succeeds through the service API. Which principle is not satisfied?
options: Complete mediation of the consequential operation
Separation of duties between two change approvers
Minimization of retained audit-event fields
Physical diversity of the application's redundant hosts
explanations: An alternate path bypasses the intended authorisation decision.
Incorrect. The direct defect is that one access path bypasses the required authorization check, rather than an approval-role conflict.
Incorrect. Retention scope does not close an unmediated API edit path.
Incorrect. Host-site diversity addresses other failure concerns, not this missing access enforcement.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a Security Target in Common Criteria reasoning?
options: A universal list of every function all secure products must contain
A penetration-test result independent of product configuration
The operational risk acceptance for every customer deployment
The specific evaluated target’s security claims and requirements under its stated context
explanations: A target is specific rather than universal.
Configuration and claims are integral to the evaluation context.
Evaluation does not replace the customer’s acceptance decision.
The claim is tied to a defined target and environment.

questions.prompt: A Protection Profile is most appropriately understood as what?
options: A customer’s complete live configuration backup
A product-specific implementation claim tied only to one named version
A reusable requirements expression for a class of targets under the scheme
A guarantee that every product in the class has identical security features
explanations: Requirements and configuration backup serve different purposes.
Incorrect. A Protection Profile describes requirements for a class or type; a Security Target is product-specific in the evaluation context.
It captures a class-level security requirements problem rather than one complete deployment.
Products and evaluated configurations can differ within applicable requirements.

questions.prompt: An evaluated product is deployed with a new unevaluated plugin and changed operating conditions. What should the assessor do?
options: Assume the evaluation report has become false for its original configuration
Check whether the deployment remains within the evaluated scope and obtain evidence for differences
Treat the plugin vendor’s feature list as equivalent to evaluation evidence
Transfer the original assurance claim automatically because the brand is unchanged
explanations: The original scoped claim may remain valid while not covering the new deployment.
Scope and assumptions determine applicability to the changed system.
Feature descriptions are not equivalent to the required assurance evidence.
Brand identity does not establish version/configuration equivalence.

questions.prompt: Which evidence is necessary to support a cryptographic-module validation claim for a deployment?
options: Only an unrelated algorithm test certificate from another component
Only the application’s statement that it uses a standard algorithm
The applicable module record, boundary, version, environment and approved configuration
Only a successful encrypted connection in one functional test
explanations: Evidence must correspond to the actual component and claim.
Algorithm use alone is not module validation.
Validation applies to a specific scoped module and conditions.
Functional success does not establish validation status or scope.

questions.prompt: A formal protocol proof excludes endpoint compromise and implementation side channels. How should it be used?
options: As evidence for its stated model/property, alongside evidence for excluded deployment risks
As evidence that endpoint protection is unnecessary
As proof that the whole organisation cannot suffer a breach
As a replacement for all implementation and integration testing
explanations: A proof supports a bounded claim under assumptions.
Excluded risks still need treatment.
The organisation contains many elements outside the model.
Model-to-implementation and integration gaps remain.

questions.prompt: A firmware update changes authentication behaviour. What is the main value of maintained traceability?
options: Identifying affected requirements, assumptions, tests and acceptance evidence
Replacing the need to know the installed version
Assuming every existing test remains sufficient because the requirement identifiers are unchanged
Proving the new version is secure solely because the table exists
explanations: Traceability supports targeted impact analysis and revalidation.
Actual configuration identity is essential to meaningful evidence.
Incorrect. Traceability helps assess affected requirements and evidence when behavior changes; unchanged IDs do not guarantee coverage.
Links do not themselves prove the new behaviour.

questions.prompt: A degraded operating mode grants limited read access for 30 minutes during an identity-service outage. What must be explicit? Select all that apply.
options: Permitted actions and prohibited authority
An unlimited write bypass for every user who claims an emergency
Duration, observation and return-to-normal conditions
The responsible approval and residual-risk owner
explanations: The exception must be bounded in capability.
Unlimited self-declared privilege contradicts a bounded degraded mode.
Time and transition conditions prevent indefinite uncontrolled degradation.
Authority and risk acceptance remain accountable.

questions.prompt: A ticket-closure metric improves while unresolved high-consequence defects increase. What is the appropriate interpretation?
options: Activity throughput is not sufficient evidence of risk reduction or control effectiveness
Security metrics should never include outcome evidence
The defects no longer matter once the metric target is met
More closures necessarily prove lower residual risk
explanations: Measures need connection to consequence and evidence quality.
Outcome evidence is central to meaningful assessment.
A performance target does not remove real defects.
Closure counts can reflect weak scope or criteria.

questions.prompt: A supplier factory test passed. Which claim still needs site evidence?
options: The tested component produced the recorded result in that setup
The integrated system meets site-specific dependencies and acceptance conditions
The supplier performed the recorded factory test under its stated setup
The factory report can contribute to an assurance argument
explanations: The recorded scoped result is distinct from a site-wide conclusion.
Site integration introduces configuration and environmental conditions not necessarily covered at the factory.
This narrower claim may be supported by a trustworthy report.
Factory evidence can contribute without proving everything.

questions.prompt: A security exception lacks an owner and review trigger. What is the principal governance defect?
options: Its record format alone determines whether the risk is acceptable
Every exception is prohibited regardless of the business context
Its existence automatically proves a technical exploit occurred
Its continued authority and residual risk cannot be reliably revisited and accepted
explanations: Risk and evidence matter more than the document format alone.
Authorised risk decisions can include justified bounded exceptions.
A governance gap does not itself establish exploitation.
Accountability and bounded review are needed to manage accepted deviations.

questions.prompt: A read-only monitoring application retains unrestricted controller write credentials. What should the trust model recognise?
options: Network encryption converts unrestricted credentials into least privilege
The application can act as a consequential control-authority dependency despite its nominal purpose
Only the dashboard viewer’s role matters
The read-only business label removes all write authority
explanations: Encryption protects transport, not the scope of permitted operations.
Actual capability determines trust and consequence.
Backend identities and management paths also matter.
A label does not constrain credentials or execution paths.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a useful assurance case from an unsupported claim?
options: An inspectable argument linking scoped claims to relevant evidence and assumptions
A claim with no stated operating environment
A declaration that all tests are confidential so no conclusion can be challenged
A list of implemented controls without evidence linking them to the stated claims and assumptions
explanations: The reasoning and evidence must be assessable within a defined scope.
Unstated conditions make the claim difficult to evaluate.
Sensitive evidence can be controlled while still enabling authorised scrutiny.
Incorrect. Control presence alone is not a reasoned evidence-based assurance argument.

questions.prompt: Hardware is retired but its service account and trusted certificate remain active. What lifecycle requirement was missed?
options: Removal or controlled retention of associated information and authority
Only the replacement server’s performance benchmark
The assumption that deleting hardware automatically revokes external credentials
Only completion of the physical disposal record
explanations: Retirement includes logical dependencies, credentials and records.
Replacement performance does not remove old credentials.
External systems can retain authority after hardware removal.
Incorrect. Physical disposition does not automatically revoke external identities, keys or certificates.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best represents a reasoned acceptance argument?
options: Allocate design and implementation controls
Establish need and requirement
Collect scoped verification/validation evidence
Authorised owner decides on acceptance and residual risk
explanations: Controls implement the allocated properties.
Needs define the purpose of the claim.
Evidence assesses conformance and suitability.
Acceptance follows an accountable review of evidence and remaining risk.

questions.prompt: Which route is selected for 10.40.8.15 in this simplified table?

The transport source port must become the router's forwarding interface number

Routers build link-appropriate framing while forwarding the IP packet.

questions.prompt: A firewall permits TCP443. Which conclusion requires additional evidence?
options: The rule can match the stated transport destination port
The application request is authorised and semantically safe
The rule refers to TCP rather than UDP
A matching packet can be considered under that rule’s action
explanations: This is the narrow field named by the rule.
Port selection is not application-level permission or content assurance.
The stated protocol identifies TCP.
Actual processing depends on rule order/state, but the field can match.

questions.prompt: Two VLANs have unrestricted inter-VLAN routing. What has not been established?

The required isolation between their workloads
A configured routed path between the VLANs
The existence of separate layer 2 broadcast domains under the design
explanations: An appropriate enforcement point can add policy.
Separate VLAN labels do not deny routed communication.
The scenario explicitly supplies routing.
VLANs can separate broadcast domains while allowing routed traffic.

questions.prompt: Why can a nominally air-gapped controller network still have transfer risk?

Physical separation prevents every malicious local action
Maintenance media, laptops or other interfaces may bridge the boundary
An air-gap label automatically disables all wireless hardware
explanations: Routing absence is narrower than absence of all information transfer.
Local access and removable artifacts can still matter.
Actual transfer paths and workflows must be inventoried and controlled.
Labels do not configure or remove interfaces.

questions.prompt: A workload can assign itself a trusted policy label used for micro-segmentation. Which authority needs protection?
options: Who may assign or change the labels that grant connectivity
Only the policy syntax that consumes the label
Only logging the label after a connection has already been permitted
Only the lifetime of the workload's current connection
explanations: Policy inputs can confer authority and must be governed.
Incorrect. Correct policy syntax cannot make a self-asserted trust attribute reliable.
Incorrect. Observing an attacker-controlled label does not constrain its trusted assignment.
Incorrect. Connection duration does not protect the authority to issue a trusted classification.

questions.prompt: The forward flow crosses A and the reply crosses B, which lacks shared state. What is a plausible stateful-firewall failure?
options: A’s state automatically exists in B without a synchronisation design
B rejects the reply because it cannot associate it with an allowed connection
The return packet proves the application completed its transaction
B necessarily authenticates the user from the route alone
explanations: State replication is an explicit system capability.
Asymmetric paths can miss required state under the implementation.
A return packet is not proof of business completion.
Routing does not establish user identity.

questions.prompt: A service is denied over IPv4 but reachable over IPv6. What should the assessment conclude?
options: The intended service policy has an address-family coverage gap
IPv6 cannot carry the same application service
DNS records alone enforce the missing authorisation
The IPv4 denial proves complete isolation
explanations: Both paths must satisfy the intended boundary.
Applications can operate over both address families.
Name resolution is not the complete traffic/operation policy.
One tested path cannot establish another untested path.

questions.prompt: Why is blocking every ICMPv6 message a risky default design?
options: Some ICMPv6 functions are necessary for normal neighbour and path behaviour
A blanket block proves neighbour identity authenticity
IPv6 automatically replaces all ICMPv6 with ARP
ICMPv6 is only an optional diagnostic echo protocol
explanations: Policy must distinguish required protocol functions from unwanted exposure.
Dropping a protocol does not authenticate neighbours.
IPv6 neighbour functions do not simply use IPv4 ARP.
ICMPv6 includes more than echo diagnostics.

questions.prompt: An overlay encapsulates tenant traffic. Which security property should not be assumed from encapsulation alone?
options: The presence of an additional protocol wrapper
Additional header overhead affecting effective MTU
Payload confidentiality and application authorisation
A relationship between overlay and underlay delivery
explanations: Encapsulation adds a wrapper by definition.
Extra headers consume space on the path.
A wrapper is not automatically encryption or permission enforcement.
The underlay carries the encapsulated traffic.

questions.prompt: Small probes succeed through a tunnel while larger transfers stall. Which hypothesis deserves targeted testing?

The existence of any route is impossible
Every successful probe proves all application sizes work
The remote application must use the same segment size as the successful small probe
explanations: Size-dependent failure can arise from effective MTU and discovery handling.
Small traffic success shows at least some forwarding path exists.
A small probe tests only its own size and behaviour.
Incorrect. A small probe does not establish that larger packets fit the encapsulated path or that discovery works.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts UDP with TCP?
options: UDP lacks TCP’s reliable byte-stream connection semantics; applications may add their own reliability/security
Using UDP proves packet delivery is ordered and complete
UDP can never carry an authenticated application
TCP automatically authorises every business operation
explanations: Transport behaviour and application security are different layers.
UDP itself does not supply those TCP-like guarantees.
Authenticated protocols can use UDP.
TCP delivery does not grant business authority.

questions.prompt: What does anycast selection depend on in an IP network?

A broadcast delivered to every host on the link
A requirement that all instances share identical live application state
A guarantee of the physically closest server by distance
explanations: Routing determines the selected path/instance under its conditions.
Anycast and broadcast have different delivery semantics.
Application state consistency requires a separate design.
Topology and policy need not follow geographic distance.

questions.prompt: Which observations belong in a defensible segmentation test? Select all that apply.
options: Alternate management/address-family paths follow the same intended policy
A permitted application flow completes under the expected identity
A successful ping is treated as proof of every application permission
A prohibited flow is denied at the intended enforcement point
explanations: Alternate paths can bypass a narrowly tested control.
Positive behaviour verifies necessary service function.
ICMP reachability is not a complete application-authorisation test.
Negative behaviour tests the boundary.

questions.prompt: A network sensor sees encrypted transport metadata but cannot inspect protected payload. What is the accurate report?

Claim payload content was inspected because the port is known
Describe the observable metadata and the payload visibility limit
Declare endpoint/application evidence irrelevant
explanations: Malicious or unauthorised actions can use encryption.
Port identification does not decrypt content.

Other evidence can address visibility gaps.

questions.prompt: Two dedicated management VLANs use the same failed switch control plane as production. Which claim is not established?

Dependence on the shared switching platform
The possibility that a separate physical design could improve independence
Independence of management access from that production failure
explanations: Configured VLAN separation can exist despite shared infrastructure.
The scenario states a common control-plane dependency.

Logical separation alone does not remove the shared failure dependency.

A guarantee that backend authorisation is unnecessary
A rule that the proxy cannot observe credentials
Both channel boundaries and the proxy’s plaintext/identity authority

Application permission remains necessary.
A terminating proxy may access plaintext under the design.
Termination creates distinct protection and trust scopes.

The inability of TLS to protect any ordinary record
Automatic disclosure of every certificate private key
Repeated execution despite encrypted transport
explanations: Actual effects matter; method labels do not prove idempotency.
The concern is scoped to early-data semantics, not a total failure of TLS.
Replay risk does not imply private-key disclosure.
Early-data replay properties need application-level analysis and controls.

questions.prompt: A VPN association is up, but a new remote subnet is unreachable. Which evidence should be checked?

Only the green tunnel-status icon
Traffic selectors, routes, translations and policy for the specific flow
Only a successful ping between the tunnel endpoints themselves

The icon provides a narrower state indication.
Association establishment does not prove coverage of every flow.

Always bidirectional with no separate reverse state
A routing-table entry that identifies every protected subnet
Unidirectional; corresponding state supports the opposite direction
explanations: Incorrect. A security association is protocol security state, not an application authorization account.
Bidirectional communication uses corresponding associations/state.

Tunnel mode necessarily encrypts every outer routing field
The word IPsec alone proves the deployed traffic policy is correct
AH encrypts every payload while ignoring packet integrity

Outer delivery headers remain needed for routing and have defined treatment.
Correct coverage and policy need evidence.
AH is an integrity/authentication mechanism, not payload encryption.

The error path can remove intended peer authentication
A successful retry proves the original error was harmless
Disabling validation automatically improves certificate revocation
explanations: The validation check has explicitly been removed.
The alternate path weakens a required property.
Success under weaker checks does not resolve the underlying cause.
Revocation is not improved by skipping validation.

Verify the authorised rebuild/key change through a trusted process before accepting the new identity
Always accept because rebuilds can change keys
Always declare a confirmed interception without checking evidence

The observation alone does not prove attack.

Only whether shell commands are restricted while forwarding remains unrestricted
Only whether the SSH host key successfully authenticates the gateway
Only whether the forwarded bytes remain inside an encrypted SSH channel

The confidentiality of every prior packet necessarily
Time-bounded operational authorisation/session enforcement
The supplier’s ability to prove possession of its login factor necessarily
explanations: MFA can work while session governance fails.

Successful authentication does not grant indefinite authority.
The factors may have been valid at login.

Any successful handshake proves all business operations are permitted
VPN negotiation succeeds while a flow is outside its selectors
TLS succeeds but the API denies an unauthorised action

Handshake success is not universal application authority.
Association state and traffic-policy coverage differ.
A protected authenticated channel can carry a legitimate permission denial.

Only the absence of a longer TLS encryption key on direct client connections
TLS encryption always prevents header spoofing after termination
All reverse proxies are inherently unable to authenticate users

Incorrect. Stronger channel encryption does not make a client-supplied operator header an authoritative identity assertion.
Termination and alternate paths require their own trust enforcement.
Proxies can participate in sound authentication when properly integrated.

questions.prompt: Which trade-off belongs in a split-tunnel remote-access decision?

A claim that split tunnelling always disables encryption on every flow
A claim that full tunnelling removes endpoint compromise risk
A requirement that DNS behaviour can be ignored in either design
explanations: The actual routed paths and dependencies need a risk-based design.
Selected tunnelled flows can remain encrypted.
Full tunnelling does not make the endpoint trustworthy.
DNS paths can affect leakage, resolution and policy.

Initial establishment proves all future key transitions
Only repeating initial tunnel establishment without crossing a rekey boundary
Rekey failures are unrelated to secure-channel availability
explanations: Normal operation includes renewal/rekey and recovery transitions.
One successful state does not prove later transitions.
Incorrect. The missing test concerns the later key-state transition, not initial establishment again.
Failure to maintain security state can interrupt the channel.

A public key automatically becomes secret when forwarded
A remote environment may gain access to signing capability through the forwarded agent
Key-file non-exposure proves no credential misuse is possible

Operation capability can matter without extraction of raw key bytes.
Use authority and secret extraction are distinct threats.

A controlled trusted pin-update path with tested continuity and failure behaviour
Treating a pin mismatch as proof the application data is already compromised

Suppressing identity errors removes the intended protection.
Pin lifecycle must preserve trust while supporting authorised change.
Mismatch indicates a trust decision problem, not automatic proof of data compromise.

The responsible process owner’s approved change scope and operating/recovery conditions
Only whether the VPN user has a successful authenticated session
A belief that encrypted commands cannot have unsafe physical effects

The SSID text matching a remembered name
A hidden SSID advertisement setting

Every authentication server function simultaneously
Authorisation result mapping/enforcement at the edge
The negotiated radio data rate rather than the returned and enforced authorization role

Because matching the SSID is sufficient even if the server certificate names another service
To ensure the client never needs its own credential

The MAC address is an unexportable private key

Compatibility admission proves current endpoint health

A link-layer address is not a cryptographic private key.
Needed access should be bounded by function and risk.
Address matching does not establish software/process health.

Only the AP’s maximum advertised data rate
An assumption that all legacy clients acquire every modern property
Only the dashboard’s WPA3 family label

Legacy capability does not change by assumption.
A family label can conceal per-client negotiated differences.

options: That the implementation needs compatible client support
That configuration and negotiation still need validation
That defined management traffic receives protection under the negotiated mode
That radio jamming and every pre-association threat are eliminated

Operational verification remains necessary.
This is the appropriately scoped purpose.
The mechanism has a bounded protocol scope and cannot remove physical interference.

questions.prompt: Which tests belong in NAC lifecycle validation? Select all that apply.

Authentication-service outage and the resulting assigned role
Certificate renewal and reauthentication
Revocation or role change for an already established session
explanations: Termination behaviour is implementation-specific and must be tested.
Failure behaviour can alter access.
Credential lifecycle can affect admission and continuity.

Only a channel inventory with no observed roaming and reauthentication behavior
Roaming/authentication/policy transition timing with representative clients
A second stationary speed test alone

That the design can include separate network policy
Strong radio encryption and trustworthy endpoint posture
That access may be subject to a guest-use process

Network policy can complement the portal.
A web workflow is not equivalent to link protection or endpoint trust.

That customer endpoint responsibilities remain relevant
That the service may have defined connectivity policy
That a carrier service arrangement exists if contracted
explanations: The service label does not prove complete isolation/encryption for the application.
